chapter_theme: On the way to the altar of Chandamari the two youths meditate on the five objects of their reverence, are brought before the king with the sword drawn, bless him while smiling, and, asked why they laugh, tell him that fear is useless and that harm to living bodies bears suffering through births; the king lays down the sword and asks for their story, and the youth begins a sermon on karma, the body's filth and the rejection of those who deny rebirth.
structure_note: 51-56 are the youths' meditation on the Jain's five objects of reverence; 57-60 the scene at the altar; 61-67 the king's questions and his turn; 68-73 the start of the youth's sermon.

cast.role: the two young ascetics, brother and sister, brought to be sacrificed to the goddess
the young ascetic who speaks for the pair and preaches to the king
the king who has the youths brought to the goddess's altar and then lays down his sword
the man who brings the youths to the altar of Chandamari
the people of the earth present at the altar, who hear the youth and marvel

51.reading: The two youths, walking to their death, tell themselves that they have won the rare wealth of the three jewels, which makes an end of birth, gives greatness over the world and is known through knowledge.
51.nuance: The verse names the jewels as one word and does not list them; that they are right faith, knowledge and conduct is the Jain tradition, not something these lines say. The poem opens the five verses of meditation (51-56) that the youths hold on the way.
51.event: The two youths, going toward the sacrifice, take stock of what they have gained.

claims.claim: the three jewels (அரதனத் திரயம்) give greatness and bring the release that cuts off birth

52.reading: Calling to mind the liberated ones at the crest-jewel of the world, who stand free of the wide ruin of karma with their eight qualities and have put away every harm, the youths take them as the ones who end their sorrow.
52.nuance: Verses 52-56 read as the five objects of a Jain's reverence (liberated souls, arhats, teachers, preceptors, ascetics); the Tamil names none of the five by that count, and the order here begins with the liberated ones, not the arhats. Siddhar here (சித்தர்) means the liberated, not the Tamil Siddhar poets.

claims.claim: the liberated ones, freed from karma and possessed of eight qualities, are the refuge that ends sorrow

53.reading: The youths think next of the teaching lords who, having driven out the great enemy of the destroying karmas and gained the fourfold wealth, are yet a single lamp to every soul and end its sorrows with their holy word.
53.nuance: காதி (the destroying karmas) and நான்மைத் திரு (the fourfold wealth) are read from the Jain tradition's terms; the verse gives no count. The number printed before the verse is a misprint for 53.

claims.claim: the teaching lords who have driven out the destroying karmas end the sorrows of souls by their word

54.reading: They think of the first teachers, who spread the fivefold conduct, a rare vessel, among the worthy as they follow it themselves, showing the true path and so wiping out the harm that sorrow rests on.
54.nuance: பவ்வியர் (the fit for release) is a Jain term for souls able to reach it; the verse uses it without gloss.

claims.claim: teachers who show the true path and teach the fivefold conduct to the fit remove sorrow

55.reading: They think of those who learned the Anga and other scriptures free of fault, argued by the seven standpoints, and took the nectar of the true text into themselves; these give to the youths, and are the ones who wash their karma.
55.nuance: பங்கமேழ் பங்கம் (line 2) is read here as the seven-fold method of argument; the line is compressed and the reading could turn on it, so only the main sense is relied on.

claims.claim: those who master the scriptures and teach them wash away the hearers' karma

56.reading: They end with the ascetics, who are vessels fit for the great form, hold only to good qualities and think of no other path than the Jina's; apart from such holy men, they ask, who is a refuge for them in the world?
56.nuance: சேதியின் நெறியின் வேறு (line 3) can be read as 'other than the Jina's path' or as a reference to a shrine; the ascetics' exclusive loyalty is clear either way.

claims.claim: only the ascetics of the true path are a refuge for the world

57.reading: Having gone on with such thoughts, the youths are quickly led by Chandan to the altar in front of the gate of the fierce Chandamari, and as they stand the king speaks in his delight.
57.nuance: Line 2 (தனையரசருளும் பெற்றிச் சண்டன்) is compressed; Chandan is taken as the one who brings the youths, a role his place in the scene supports but the line does not state outright.
57.event: Chandan brings the two youths to the altar of Chandamari's gate, and the king, pleased, begins to speak.

58.reading: Someone urges the king, crusher of armies, that the deed of offering a man to the goddess is good for him today, and the king leads the two into the goddess's great place of sacrifice and, alas, draws his sword.
58.nuance: Lines 1-2 are an address to the king and seem to be the advice of whoever brought the youths; Chandan is the likeliest, but the verse does not name him, and the sentence runs on into the narrator's lament (ஐயோ). The claim is tagged general because the goddess cult of Chandamari fits none of the listed schools. The work answers it in this chapter: verse 63 gives the cost of killing and 71 says the dharma cuts cruelty down.
58.event: The king brings the youths to the goddess's sacrificial ground and draws his sword.

claims.claim: a man given in sacrifice to the goddess is a good deed for the king

59.reading: At the place of killing the two stand unshaken, their bodies marked by their virtues; told to say 'may the king live long', these men of spotless mind answer only with an empty smile.
59.nuance: The command in line 3 is spoken by someone the verse does not name; the smile (வறியதோர் முறுவல்) can mean a bare smile or one with nothing behind it, and verse 63 later says what it hid.
59.event: At the killing ground the youths are told to wish the king long life, and they smile.

60.reading: Not tormenting any living thing in forgetfulness, they say, let the king take the holy dharma that ends the prison of birth, spread mercy to every precious life and so guard the world of full fame and live long.
60.nuance: The blessing is a condition as much as a wish: 'long life' is tied to what the king does, so the youths give the answer to the order in verse 59 without refusing it.
60.event: The youths bless the king with the wish that he keep to mercy.

claims.claim: a king who harms no life and spreads mercy to all will guard the world and live long
the holy dharma ends the confinement of birth

61.reading: The king, his firm resolve slackening, asks whether these bodies bright as lightning are vidyadharas or gods, since such a form is rare among men on earth and their steadiness is beyond thought.
61.nuance: நிலைதளர் நீதி மன்னன் shows the first slackening of the king's purpose: wonder, not yet mercy.
61.event: The king, shaken, asks who the two are.

62.reading: Asked why they laugh without trembling when danger has come, they answer that if what must come will come, fear has no use, and so they stood without a tremor, clear in the good dharma.
62.nuance: Verse 63 then gives the cause of what 'must come'; here the ground of the calm is only that fear changes nothing.
62.event: The king asks why they laugh; the youth says fear has no use against what is due.

claims.claim: fear is of no use against what must come

63.reading: The youth says that through harm they once did to the bodies of living beings they have met sufferings in birth after birth, and they laughed within themselves wondering what could come of a wish for long life for a king who kills creatures.
63.nuance: The deed is the doers' own harm to living bodies, and no god or fate is named as sending it; the youths count themselves among those it fell on.
63.event: The youth explains why they laughed.

claims.claim: sin done by harming the bodies of living beings in earlier lives brings sufferings through birth after birth
a wish of long life for a king who kills creatures can bear no good fruit

64.reading: The people present, hearing the youth's sweet speech to its end, say that a man's courage is fitting and beautiful, but that this woman's courage, like a queen's, is hard to put into words.
64.nuance: The speakers of line 3-4 are taken as the people the king's court holds; பெண்ணினுக்கு அரசி can also be read as a name or title for the girl, and the unit does not fix it.
64.event: The onlookers marvel at the pair, and at the girl above all.

65.reading: Pleased by what he heard, the king asks them to tell the births that went before, the family in which they were born, and why they came to him as they are.
65.event: The king asks to hear of their births and their lineage.

66.reading: The youth says that his words do not enter as meaning in deluded, cruel men but only in those of merciful mind who love dharma, and bids the king, if he truly wants them, to do an act of mercy first.
66.nuance: அருளியல் செய்து செல்க (line 4) is read as 'act with mercy, then go on'; it may also mean 'grant mercy and go forward', either of which is the king's turn from the sword.
66.event: The youth makes mercy a condition of the telling.

claims.claim: teaching takes hold only in those of merciful mind who love dharma, not in the deluded and cruel

67.reading: At this the king, softened, puts aside the sword in his hand and the cruelty in his mind, bows, calls the youth his lord from now, and asks him to tell of his births along with his compassion.
67.nuance: மனத்தியை மறனும் (line 2) is read மனத்து இயை மறனும், the cruelty joined to his mind.
67.event: The king lays down the sword, bows, and asks to hear their account.

68.reading: Like a cloud with lightning that comes before the golden mountain and pours rain to end the earth's affliction, the prince begins to rain the dharma on the king.
68.nuance: Line 3 is a compressed simile of the listener melting beside a swan-gaited woman and is not relied on.
68.event: The youth begins to preach dharma to the king.

69.reading: The youth tells the king that his inner worth is great and fair, and says he will answer in order all that the king asked, if the king listens with a steady mind.
69.event: The youth promises to answer the king's questions in order.

70.reading: As far as they hear this, he says, it checks the influx of karma and makes it shed, and, for those who have learned the true kinds and shrink from the other way, it makes them ripe for release, O king.
70.nuance: The words ஊற்றுச் செறித்து உதிர்ப்பை read as the Jain pair of stopping the inflow of karma and shedding it; the line is compressed and the subject of the verbs is carried over from the preceding words, so the sense is probable, not fixed.
70.event: The youth tells the king what hearing the dharma does for a hearer.

claims.claim: hearing the dharma checks the influx of karma, brings its shedding and ripens the hearer for release

71.reading: The dharma, he goes on, turns aside the notions that rise in the mind in the body's hut full of filth, destroys desire in the pleasures of the senses, cuts down the cruelty of killing, and does harm to the love of women with bow-like brows.
71.nuance: Line 4 can be read as the dharma harming the love of women (curing the hearer) or as that love doing harm; the first sits better with the three lines before it.

claims.claim: the body is a hut full of filth
the dharma destroys desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing

72.reading: Some have said that those born gain fruit by their own effort alone, that the dead are not born again, and that there are no two deeds; the youth calls this lack of knowledge and tells the king to leave it and strive on the dharma's road.
72.nuance: The denial is reported as a summary in the youth's mouth, which the materialists themselves might not word so. It is dismissed as ignorance here and answered by the account of his own births that verse 73 promises.

claims.claim: the born gain fruit by their own effort only, the dead are not reborn and there are no two deeds

73.reading: The youth says that the sight that yields dharma's wealth did not come only through the great ascetics' grace but also from knowing his own births and understanding them anew, and asks the king to put his clear faith in it; all gladly begin to listen.
73.nuance: அருளிற்றன்றி (line 1) may mean 'not only through' or 'not through' the ascetics' grace; the more guarded sense is used.
73.event: All present are bidden to hear and begin to listen gladly.

claims.claim: the right sight that gives rise to dharma can come from knowing one's own earlier births, not from the ascetics' teaching alone

links.note: Kural 259 ranks refusing to take and eat one creature's life above a thousand oblations; verse 58 shows the rite at its far end, a man led to the goddess's place with the king's sword drawn.
links.teaches: The couplet weighs a ritual's merit against one life in general; the epic puts the weighing at the altar, where the offering is a man and the weigher is the king holding the sword.

gains.a: the sacrifice is seen to be what a Tamil couplet already ranks below a single creature's life
gains.b: the couplet's thousand sacrifices gain a concrete victim and a king's hand

links.note: Naladiyar 16 sets a kid nibbling the leaf garland before it in the fierce ritual ground; verse 59 sets two youths at the place of killing, smiling.
links.teaches: The kid is glad because it does not know where it stands, while the youths' smile at the same kind of place rests on knowing, so the doomed creature's calm turns from ignorance to composure.

gains.a: the youths' smile is read against a stock image of unknowing gladness and shown to be its opposite
gains.b: the kid's gladness gains a counter-case, one who sees the killing ground and is not shaken

links.note: Bhadragiriyar longs for the day he will stop killing and eating lives and hold them as his own life; in verse 60 the two at the killing ground wish the king to spread mercy to every life.
links.teaches: The Siddhar states mercy as a vow about his own food and conduct; the epic has it spoken as a blessing by the victims to the one holding the sword.

gains.a: the blessing is shown to carry an ethic a Siddhar names as the aim of his tapas, so mercy is the road and not a courtesy
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to see lives as his own gains a scene where the victim does so for the man about to kill him

links.note: Verse 36 grieves over the bodies taken in each birth; verse 63 gives the youth's cause for the suffering, harm done to living bodies.
links.teaches: The earlier verse only laments births; this one names harming living creatures as what the sufferings come from.

links.note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; the youth traces the pair's sufferings over many births to harm done to living bodies.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the deed's aim but not its kind; the epic names the kind, injury to living beings, and spreads its return over many births.

gains.a: the youth's account is given a Tamil image of how a deed finds its doer
gains.b: the old deed gains a named kind, harm to living bodies, and a span of many births

links.note: Pattinattar confesses to killing and eating many lives and trusts the Lord to bear the fault; the youth holds that harm to living bodies brings suffering through births.
links.teaches: Whether the guilt of killing can be borne by another turns on whether a god stands in the account: the verse sets a chain of sin and suffering with no pardoner in it, while the poet's plea counts on one.

gains.a: the youth's law of deeds is set against a pardon a Saiva poet counts on
gains.b: the poet's trust in the Lord is seen as a step outside a doctrine where the harm simply follows the doer

links.note: Verse 46 asks whether there is fear in leaving this life of fearful births; verse 62 shows the youths without trembling at the killing ground.
links.teaches: The earlier fearlessness was a resolve made in a garden of talk; here it is tested at the place of death.

links.note: In verse 58 the king draws his sword at the goddess's place; in verse 67 he puts the sword in his hand aside.
links.teaches: The same sword marks the king's turn: first the instrument of offering, then what he sets down when the youth's mercy reaches him.

links.note: Verse 70 says hearing the dharma checks karma's influx and sheds it; Tirumanthiram 1527 says grace comes as the guru and, when one's own doing ends through the knowledge it gives, the three impurities end.
links.teaches: Both make a teacher's word the means of release, but in one the hearer's own checking and shedding does the work, and in the other his own doing must cease and grace does it.

gains.a: the Jain account of release by the hearer's own stopping and shedding is set against a rival where grace comes as a guru
gains.b: Tirumular's 'when one's own doing ends' meets a doctrine where one's own effort is the whole means, sharpening what it denies

links.note: Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone to cure desire; verse 71 calls the body a hut of filth and the dharma what ends desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing.
links.teaches: The quatrain cures desire by looking at the parts; the epic ties the same look to a dharma that also ends killing, so the contemplation of foulness shares a root with the mercy that stays the king's sword.

gains.a: the body-as-filth gains a concrete inventory of parts, which the epic names only as filth
gains.b: the quatrain's disgust is set in a system joining it to non-killing and release, not only restraint of lust

links.note: Neelakesi 859 gives the materialist's own words, that the world is only the elements and belief in a soul only makes fruitless quarrels; verse 72 gives the denial in one summary and calls it ignorance.
links.teaches: The same opponent appears as a speaker in one poem and as a target in the other, so the epic's verdict can be set beside the debating poem's long hearing.

links.note: Verse 49 holds the soul to be other than the body that joins it; verse 72 reports those who say the dead are not reborn.
links.teaches: The denial in 72 is the denial of the premise 49 had stated, so the dismissal there rests on a claim made earlier in the book.

new_concepts.gloss: the three jewels, the Jain triad whose possession gives release from birth
the teaching lords who show the way across birth, whose word ends the sorrow of souls
the offering of a man in sacrifice to a goddess

source_issues: Verse 53: the number is printed as 3; read as 53.
Verse 67, line 2: மனத்தியை is read மனத்து இயை.
Verse 58: lines 1-2 and 3-4 seem to have different speakers; the verse is read as advice followed by the narrator's lament.
